en.title: watchOS 27: A Summary of VoiceOver Features, Issues, and Improvements
en.summary: Apple has today released watchOS 27 to the public. watchOS 27 is compatible with the Apple Watch Series 9 and later and the Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later. Due to the inherent challenges of beta software testing on watchOS, our testing of watchOS 27 has been quite limited. That said, for VoiceOver users, there is at least one new bug that we are aware of and a handful of new features and improvements. New VoiceOver Bugs in watchOS 27 There is rather significant latency with VoiceOver speech when swiping through the user interface. Specifically, there is a delay between when the VoiceOver sound effects/haptics play, and when VoiceOver speaks. Our testing suggests that this issue is not synthesizer-specific. It is unclear to us whether this behavior is simply a function of the newer operating system encountering the limits of hardware (something that has historically been a challenge on Apple Watch devices), or whether this is something that can be resolved by Apple in a future software update. A Feedback report has been filed, and we will keep the community advised as additional information becomes available. If you identify any additional vision accessibility bugs in watchOS 27, please let us know by posting a comment. New VoiceOver Features and Improvements in watchOS 27 There is a new "Tap to Wake" toggle in VoiceOver settings. By default, the setting is enabled, and the Watch will be woken when you tap on the screen. Our best understanding is that disabling this feature should prevent the device from waking when the screen is tapped. It is now possible to customize the speaking of VoiceOver hints in watchOS. Available options are 'Always', 'Never', and 'App-Specific Hints'. On the Clock Face, VoiceOver now speaks the names of Complications before speaking their content. For example, VoiceOver might say, "Weather, Mostly Sunny 65 Degrees," instead of just saying "Mostly Sunny 65 Degrees." For braille display users, there is a new setting, "Translate After a Delay." There are other braille settings that we also believe may be new in this release, but our braille-related testing in watchOS is very limited and so this is not something we are able to comment on with any level of certainty. If you spot any other new features/changes in watchOS 27 or have any corrections to the above, please do let us know by posting a comment. watchOS 27 Release Notes watchOS 27 features the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, updates to Workout Buddy, a new tap gesture, a dynamic app grid to make it easier to access your most used apps, and improvements that make watchOS 27 more responsive and delightful to use. Siri AI is an entirely new version of Siri that is more intelligent, knowledgeable, and capable. With improvements that span areas like fitness, design, performance, and more, the experience on watchOS 27 has been refined and elevated, so it feels even better to use. Siri AI A more capable and conversational version of Siri is rolling out to users. It helps you find what you need and get more done, drawing on capabilities like personal context understanding, app actions, onscreen awareness, and access to broad world knowledge. New voice experience offers more expressive and natural-sounding voices, and lets you customize expressivity and pace to make Siri more personal to you using powerful on-device models on paired iPhone Air and iPhone 17 Pro models and later. Dedicated Siri app provides an easy way to revisit an existing conversation or kick off a new one, and privately syncs conversations across your Apple products with iCloud. Apple Intelligence across apps Workout Buddy delivers motivation with new insights and is now available without your iPhone nearby when you have a Wi-Fi or cellular connection. Call Context in the Phone app understands when you’re speaking to certain businesses and proactively surfaces relevant information from across your apps, like a confirmation code or a reservation number. Cycle Tracking Cycle deviation notifications that are suggestive of perimenopause can be received by those age 40 and over. Watch Faces Siri Modular face features a rectangular complication that mirrors the top widget of the Smart Stack, which dynamically updates to show the most relevant widget, as well as a Siri complication to quickly invoke Siri. Smart Stack Single-handed tap gesture enables you to tap your index finger and thumb together once to select a widget in the Smart Stack, even if your other hand is occupied. New suggestion widgets will be surfaced when most relevant to you, including a Parked Car location, birthday reminders for a close contact, balance changes on a transit card, Noise app after a loud noise notification, and more. System Improvements Dynamic app grid highlights your most popular and recently used apps. Find My app is now consolidated into one app to show People, Devices, and Items with a map-centric interface. Media playback now starts faster. Workout app makes distance calculations during treadmill workouts even more accurate from the first step of every walk or run. Fitness app features more accurate route maps after workouts. Battery extension notifications may be proactively offered to disable certain features to increase battery life, including gestures, Start Workout reminders, and Raise to Speak method of invoking Siri. Shazam in the Smart Stack and Music Recognition app identifies songs offline without an internet connection and delivers results automatically when you’re back online. Liquid Glass refinements improve readability with more uniform refraction and improved contrast. For information on the security content of Apple software updates, please visit: https://support.apple.com/100100 Usage limits may apply for some Apple Intelligence features. To learn more, please visit: https://www.apple.com/apple-intelligence Software updates, like this one, add new features and improvements that may affect performance and/or battery life. To learn more, please visit: https://support.apple.com/125039 How to Update watchOS 27 is available via Over-the-Air Update (Settings > General > Software Update) or by going to the Watch app on your iPhone and navigating to General > Software Update. To install the update, your Watch must be connected to its charger and have at least 50% battery power.

en.title: iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: A Summary of VoiceOver and Braille Issues and Improvements
en.summary: iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 will be available to the public on Monday, September 14, 2026. This post contains a summary of new bugs and fixes impacting VoiceOver and Braille support that the AppleVis Editorial Team has independently validated during our use and testing of these releases. The information contained in this post is compiled from our own use and testing of iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 during the beta period from June to September 2026; as well as from validated reports submitted by others through our Community Bug Program and shared on the AppleVis Forum. Our sincere appreciation goes to everyone who so generously took the time to share their findings with us. At the outset, we need to state explicitly that the bug list contained in this post is not definitive and that our assessments are not infallible. While we are confident in the presence of the issues discussed in this post, there are many other reports shared on the AppleVis Forum by members of our community that we have not been able to independently replicate with the available information. Many of these reports represented use cases that are different from those of our team; and a small number were issues that, despite understanding how to reproduce them, we did not get the same results. We say all of this so that readers understand the limits of our own testing, and that others' experiences may be different from ours. An issue not being present in our bug list does not mean the issue does not exist; it simply means that we are either unaware of or unable to reproduce it. As is our routine practice, each bug in this post has been given a severity rating. These ratings are based upon what we believe to be the implications for accessing and using features and functionality for the average user; the level of impact on the overall user experience; and whether or not there is an effective workaround for the issue. However, as these ratings are subjective to an extent, it is very possible that they may not reflect your own opinion or use case. With this in mind, we strongly recommend reading this full post and any replies before updating to iOS 27 and iPadOS 27; as we believe this will help you make an informed decision on whether to install the software at the current time or to wait for a future release. We also strongly recommend that you read this Megathread about the iOS 27 RC , as it contains a wealth of community reports about and experiences with the Release Candidate version of the software. Some issues listed in this post and on the Forum may manifest only under specific conditions; this is all the more likely as software continues to add more features and the number of devices, available configurations, and use cases in Apple's ecosystem continues to grow. You likely will not experience every bug that we list, and you likely will not agree with every severity rating for the bugs that you do experience. While we wish it were otherwise, this is to be expected. And as is the nature with all software, it is also likely that you will encounter issues that are not reported in this post. To ensure the information in this post is as complete and accurate as possible, we would appreciate input from those who have installed iOS 27 or iPadOS 27. Please confirm if you are encountering the same problems listed or if you have found workarounds. Please also let us know about any additional issues not mentioned here. Of course, it is even more important that you report any new bugs directly to Apple - they are already aware of the ones listed in this post. For an explanation of why and how to report bugs to Apple, see this post. With all of the preamble out of the way, below are the new bugs for VoiceOver and Braille users which members of the AppleVis Editorial Team have personally experienced and believe to be present in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: A Major Change to VoiceOver's Audio Profile In iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, there is a significant change in the sound profile of VoiceOver when the device's internal speaker is used. When compared to iOS 26, VoiceOver audio in iOS 27 has significantly less bass, particularly at lower volume levels. The resulting sound might best be described as 'neutral' or 'flat', with significantly less of the low-end emphasis and other processing that has characterized VoiceOver audio in recent versions of iOS/iPadOS. If you have not yet upgraded to iOS 27, we believe that you can get a reasonable approximation of how VoiceOver will sound on your device by making a phone call, putting the call on speaker, and then using VoiceOver to navigate around the screen; as the flatter, more neutral sound profile that VoiceOver uses during a phone call sounds very similar to what we are hearing in iOS 27. At the time of publication, we do not know whether the change to VoiceOver's sound profile is expected behavior; thus, we are not including it in our bug list. Nevertheless, we feel that users should be aware of this change before upgrading. If we receive additional information, we will update this post accordingly. Serious Bugs When the state of an item changes or the screen updates, VoiceOver does not always recognize/speak the information. This issue has many manifestations, including (but not limited to): When waking the device, VoiceOver may speak the time the device was last woken rather than the current time; When information updates onscreen (such as the status of an operation in an app), VoiceOver may not speak it right away and instead speak the previously displayed text. There is no known workaround, though VoiceOver will eventually speak the updated information if focus is moved off of and back onto the impacted element enough times. The VoiceOver Per-Voice Equalizer (a feature that allows one to customize certain frequency/tonal characteristics of a voice) does not work. There is no known workaround. If you rely on the per-voice Equalizer, we recommend that you do not install iOS/iPadOS 27 until this issue is resolved. The VoiceOver Pronunciation Dictionary does not work reliably, with custom pronunciations often not being obeyed by VoiceOver. There is no known workaround. If you rely on the Pronunciation Dictionary, we recommend that you do not install iOS/iPadOS 27 until this issue is resolved. On some devices, Sound Curtain and Touch Curtain do not work. For affected users, it is possible to partially work around the issue with Sound Curtain by setting the device volume to 0%. There is no known workaround for Touch Curtain. If you rely on Sound Curtain or Touch Curtain, we recommend that you do not install iOS/iPadOS 27 until this issue is resolved. If an external audio device is connected, VoiceOver speech does not work when playing audio in Safari. Pausing the audio causes it to start working again. Sometimes, when reading text, VoiceOver stops speaking and does not resume on its own. This issue does not occur all of the time. When it does occur, speech will stop mid-sentence (and sometimes even mid-word). Touching the screen or performing a touch gesture (like a one-finger swipe left or right) restores speech, and the user can then refocus VoiceOver on the impacted element. In iOS 27's new Recovery Menu, there is no spoken feedback in Diagnostics Mode, rendering this option completely inaccessible. There is no known workaround to make Diagnostics Mode itself usable. If you do manage to accidentally get your device into Diagnostics Mode, our experience is that the device will restart into normal operation after approximately five to ten minutes of inactivity. Moderate Bugs In Safari, the buttons to switch between the Start Page, Reading List, History, and Bookmarks do not work. It is possible to select these buttons, and VoiceOver indicates they have been selected, but the content itself does not update, meaning content cannot be reached. As a workaround, perform a one-finger triple-tap (what is known as a "long press") on the desired button to activate it. Our thanks to AppleVis user Brian Giles for this workaround. When VoiceOver focus is placed inside a text field, and then subsequently moved onto a combo box, the menu automatically opens. On occasions, when swiping through the Lock Screen using one-finger swipe right or left, VoiceOver focus may be inconsistent. When navigating through the Lock Screen using a one-finger swipe right, after the "Swipe up to Unlock" element, the expected behavior is that VoiceOver will focus on the first notification (if present); Focus status (if present); or the first item on the screen, like Flashlight or Camera. However, sometimes, VoiceOver users may find that focus is instead placed on items from the Status Bar, such as Cellular Carrier, Battery Percentage, or the Clock. If VoiceOver focus does land on items from the Status Bar when swiping, it is sometimes possible to continue swiping to the right and get to the first Lock Screen item; however, other times, VoiceOver focus can become stuck in a loop between the time, the "Swipe Up to Unlock" element, Cellular Carrier, an element with no spoken or audible feedback, or any combination of the above. Sometimes, VoiceOver does not speak the time when the device is woken with the Side Button. If this issue occurs, single-tap the screen with one finger to wake the device. After prompting Siri with the Side button, revealing the interface at the top of the screen, nothing happens when double-tapping the "Open in App" button. Double-tapping this button should work to activate it, opening the conversation in the Siri app. In the Phone App, the buttons to switch between 'All' and 'Missed' do not work. This issue can be worked around by either switching to Unified View or swiping through all calls in Classic View. Sometimes, it is not possible to access notifications with VoiceOver that are visually displayed onscreen. Typically, the 'Show notifications' button is present, but on these intermittent occasions, selecting it fails to reveal the notifications, and does nothing. If this issue occurs, double-tap and hold on the "Show Notifications" button, and swipe up. This will reveal the notifications. In Notification Center, the option to clear all notifications does not work. A consistent workaround for this issue has not been identified at the time of posting. We recommend clearing notifications manually. VoiceOver's 'Copy Speech' function copies the full semantic markup and hints, instead of just the spoken text. For example, in iOS 27, Copy Speech might paste "Latest news, heading Level 2". In previous versions of iOS, Copy Speech would only paste "Latest news," which is the desired behavior. Screen Recognition does not appear in VoiceOver's Quick Settings panel, even if selected for inclusion. The Camera App contains extraneous elements for editing Camera Controls when Edit Mode is not active. This includes "Remove" elements next to each camera control and a "Done" button that does nothing when tapped. When an app is open and VoiceOver focus is placed on the battery indicator, it is not possible to swipe to other items on the status bar. The Direct Touch option in the VoiceOver Quick Settings panel does not work. Minor Bugs On the Keypad in the Phone app, the button to place the call is labeled as "Call Answer." When focusing on a conversation in the Siri app, the Actions rotor for the conversation contains two identical "Delete" actions. When the device is set to 24-Hour Time, VoiceOver does not correctly speak the time on the top of the hour. When customising VoiceOver touch gestures and you select to replace the current command with a new one, the old command is sometimes not overwritten, necessitating manual removal and replacement. When the Safari toolbar is set to 'Bottom', the "Show Bookmarks" button is incorrectly labelled as "Bookmark." When the VoiceOver cursor reaches the first or last element onscreen in the Camera app, focus loops instead of stopping at the boundary. Improvements for VoiceOver and Braille in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 To the best of our knowledge, Apple does not routinely publish lists of bug fixes for VoiceOver or braille across releases; thus, it is difficult to get a complete accounting of every issue that has been resolved or what fixes users can expect to see upon upgrading to iOS 27 or iPadOS 27. With this in mind, our testing suggests that the following issues present in iOS/iPadOS 26 have been resolved or meaningfully improved in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: Stability of VoiceOver focus has been significantly improved across the operating system. The screen no longer locks while VoiceOver is reading a notification on the Lock Screen. Keyboard sounds once again play when VoiceOver is on, regardless of the audio ducking setting. VoiceOver focus is no longer erratic in the App Switcher when it is opened from the Home Screen. The default volume of the Eloquence speech synthesizer more closely matches that of other voices. In Conclusion Our team has compiled lists of new vision accessibility bugs for every major iOS and iPadOS release since iOS 7 in 2013. No software from any manufacturer is completely free of bugs. That said, the number of bugs - particularly those classified as 'serious' and involving core VoiceOver and braille functionality - in iOS/iPadOS 27 is deeply concerning. We call on Apple to urgently prioritize fixing the bugs listed in this post, as well as those on The AppleVis Bug Tracker . If you have not already upgraded to iOS 27 or iPadOS 27, we would strongly recommend that you take a few moments to read through any replies to this post before doing so; in case other users' experiences differ from our own. Also, consider that historically, Apple has delivered fixes for many accessibility bugs within the first few x.x.1 updates following major releases, and waiting briefly may allow Apple to resolve any initial problems reported after the public release. In the event that you do encounter an issue that is particularly bothersome, there are some troubleshooting steps you can take. Sometimes, simply toggling VoiceOver off and on again or restarting your device can resolve some issues that may arise following an OS update. Therefore, we highly recommend including these steps as part of your standard troubleshooting process. If restarting VoiceOver and/or your device does not resolve the issue, it might be worth considering a reset of your VoiceOver Settings; to do this, navigate to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Reset VoiceOver Settings. While this approach requires manually reconfiguring your customized VoiceOver settings, we have heard of multiple instances where a VoiceOver settings reset resolved issues since this feature became available in last year's iOS 26. This suggests that occasionally, problems can be attributed to local factors rather than being OS bugs. Finally, when commenting below, we ask that you please keep the discussion focused on accessibility issues specifically introduced or fixed in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27. Our release posts tend to be widely read and garner many helpful responses, so it is all the more important that readers can easily find relevant information. Also, please remember that upgrade decisions are personal, with each user's situation unique - there is no right or wrong choice. Comments criticizing others' decisions are not constructive and do nothing to add to the discussion; but they do set a negative tone and get in the way of readers finding helpful information. Furthermore, not experiencing an issue yourself does not mean that it doesn't exist for others, as bugs can be configuration-specific. Stating that an issue doesn't exist simply because you haven't encountered it is unhelpful. Our aim with these posts is to provide a forum for respectful, constructive, and honest sharing of experiences that inform decisions and empower people. In closing, we would like to again thank everyone in our community who contributed to AppleVis' testing and bug-reporting efforts during the iOS/iPadOS 27 beta cycle - be it through our Community Bug Program or just by posting on our Forum. Our information about this release is more complete because of you, and we are very grateful to all who took the time to contribute.

en.title: Brainclash
en.summary: New here? Challenge a friend, answer whenever you wish, and let the sharpest mind win. Multiple categories, and a daily reward waiting for you. Brainclash is a quiz game with a different rhythm: a refined battle of minds you take on in your own time, with no pressure. Challenge a friend to a match, let the game pair you with a random opponent, or train first against the computer. Play unfolds turn by turn: you answer, then your opponent answers, and the most accurate one wins. There's no tense timer forcing you both online at the same moment — take your turn whenever you like, and return for the next one anytime. Questions span a wide range of categories — General Knowledge, Science & Nature, History, Geography, Sports, and Arts & Entertainment — so you'll always find something that suits your interests and adds to what you know. And when a hard question comes your way, you have tools to help: remove half the options with 50:50, swap a question that doesn't suit you, or grant yourself a few extra seconds. The more you win, the higher you climb through the levels and the more coins you collect — and each day you can spin the daily wheel for a free reward. The game is made for everyone to enjoy: it works smoothly with TalkBack and VoiceOver, so screen reader users get a complete experience, crafted to be heard and not only seen. Add your friends, exchange messages between matches, and discover together who deserves the title of the smartest. Play in Arabic or English, and switch languages whenever you wish. So, are you ready to compete? Your next opponent is waiting on your move. Heading

en.title: What's new in Accessibility in iOS 27 for Blind and DeafBlind Users
en.summary: Introduction 15 years ago, I produced my first "What's New in iOS Accessibility" article. Every September since, I've been documenting what my testing of the betas has yielded. There are many welcome mainstream changes in this year's iOS 27, such as the upgraded Siri app, new parental controls, a slider to adjust Liquid Glass, further enhanced Apple Intelligence features, and much more. The new Siri has its own app, and coverage of it is beyond the scope of this article other than to mention it's much more verssitle and can assist with all kinds of tasks from asking about your personal data to recipes and so on. Lots of individuals will be reviewing these new features. As I've done for many years now, I document my findings after testing the new version of iOS throughout the summer to discuss accessibility-specific features which impact blind and DeafBlind users. Following what has become a tradition, Apple began discussing enhancements coming to accessibility with its announcement ahead of Global Accessibility Awareness Day. More info about forthcoming features was detailed during the Worldwide Developers Conference Keynote. Devices that will work with iOS 27, according to Apple are the iPhone SE 2 and later, as well as the iPhone 11 and later. The page linked to above is also a good resource for mainstream changes coming in iOS 27. VoiceOver Though there are fewer changes in iOS 27 than what were found in iOS 26, VoiceOver has gained quite a bit of new functionality. Whether you are a speech user or a braille one, there are a lot of new offerings in this year's release. Pronounce It Together There is now a setting which allows a VoiceOver user to import or share their pronunciation dictionary. This feature could be helpful when, for example, text-to-speech engines do not pronounce things correctly in local dialects. Instead of everyone having to make the changes, one person could compile it and share it with other users in a similar situation. It could also be used as a form of prank. Imagine changing the pronunciation of a friend's name to a friendly insult along with other changes and they later encounter it. These settings can be found under Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Speech> Pronunciations. Selecting 'Import' will bring up the Files function and allow the user to browse to the file they wish to import. Sharing one's own pronunciations brings up the standard Share Sheet, where the file can be sent to any number of places or contacts. Hide Your Cursor For those who may not be aware, the VoiceOver cursor appears as a black rectangular outline surrounding the item that currently has VoiceOver focus. While handy in some situations such as showing a sighted user where VoiceOver focus is set, helping a low vision user who tracks VoiceOver focus, or when demonstrating VoiceOver support to a developer, there are certainly reasons individuals may wish to disable it. This is because it can also serve as a distraction when the VoiceOver cursor itself isn't an important part of the iPhone's purpose. For example, when using the iPhone for face-to-face communication as a DeafBlind user, it can distract the person you are attempting to communicate with from the text you are typing. Some may wish to hide the visual VoiceOver cursor during screen sharing. To adjust this setting, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Cursor Visibility, and choose from showing the cursor, hiding it always, or hiding it during screen sharing. Navigating in New Ways with Explore By Touch iOS 27 brings new options to precisely control VoiceOver's reading of text when using Explore by Touch, or, as it's more commonly referred to, 'dragging your finger around the screen'. Options for Text Exploration are now Paragraph, Line, or Sentence. For example, when set to 'Sentence', VoiceOver will only speak the sentence under your finger instead of the entire element as it previously did. Users can adjust this by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Text Exploration. Note that changes made in Text Exploration only apply to Explore by Touch, and will not impact swiping through content. At least, not this particular setting. It's for Swipers Too A separate setting, called Text Navigation, offers the ability to modify how VoiceOver moves when swiping left and right through the screen with one finger. The available options are Line, Sentence, Paragraph, and Element. In addition to allowing one to more easily read blocks of text that VoiceOver sees as one large element, having these two new sets of options can give VoiceOver users other choices than the rotor for text navigation. To check out the new settings for swiping, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Text Navigation. Remember that you will need to adjust settings for Text Exploration and Text Navigation separately. Hints Become Customizable For a lot of the clients I work with who use speech, the hints offered by VoiceOver can be helpful, but there comes a point where they cause interference with touchscreen navigation once a user advances in their journey of learning VoiceOver. For example, "Double Tap to Open" can grind on one's nerves after a while. When I first started learning to use an iPhone with iOS 4, this was also something I became frustrated with. If the system hints become a nuisance, the user now has more control over them. iOS 27 brings the ability to adjust the amount of delay between when VoiceOver provides active information about what is in focus and when the hint will be conveyed. To configure this, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Verbosity> Hints, and then either type the duration in seconds ranging from 0.05 to 2.0, or use the 'Decrement' and 'Increment' buttons. The default is 0.8 seconds. It's also now possible to specify if users want all hints, app-specific hints, or no hints at all. You can find these options on the same screen. No Modifier Required for These Functions For VoiceOver commands to be assigned to keyboard shortcuts, Bluetooth keyboard users have always had to include their chosen VoiceOver modifier along with the command. This is no longer necissary with the function keys located in the top row of many Bluetooth keyboards. The setting must be enabled, which one can do by going to Settings>Accessibility>VoiceOver>Commands and setting the Switch Button for "No Modifier Keys" to on. Instead of having to press, for example, VoiceOver Modifier f8 to launch the VoiceOver Settings menu, users can now simply press F8. Live and Open for Questions Live Recognition was first integrated into VoiceOver with iOS 18. iOS 27, coupled with Apple Inteligence, gives Live Recognition even more power. Activating the 'Ask' button will allow the user to ask about what is currently in the camera's view. It's also possible to tell Live Recognition to focus on a specific thing in your environment. As long as that item is able to be tracked, its actions and movements will often be reported by VoiceOver. Ask is a feature that is highly customizable. Going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Live Recognition allows the user to set up some other options. One can change the default question asked when the button is activated, make the default input either dictation or typing, and have the Volume buttons take a still photo for a follow-up or more detailed description. Ask can be set up with a gesture, Bluetooth keyboard command, the Accessibility Shortcut, or a Perkins-style keyboard command. If none of those are what the user wants, there is also the ability to launch the Ask feature using the Action Button. It can be enabled by going to Settings> Action Button, selecting the Accessibility category, and then choosing 'Ask a Question'. The View From iOS In my view, pardon the pun, the largest upgrade for VoiceOver and braille users in iOS 27 is the massive overhaul of the Image Recognition feature. This is thanks to Apple Intelligence, but I'm sure those using iPhone 15 and earlier devices aren't feeling very thankful, since they do not have access to these features. Unlike the multi-step processes involved with using third-party services for detailed descriptions, Image Recognition descriptions typically take less than three seconds. They can be generated on virtually all images the iPhone encounters, and the user does not need to download or upload each image they wish to have described. It is also possible to describe the screen of the device itself, to ask questions about the image in focus, and to generate a description with the ability to ask a follow-up question immediately. These features can be activated through the VoiceOver rotor or by adding specific functions to gestures. The two devices I have upgraded at this point had the Image Recognition options in the Rotor. If, by chance, your Rotor does not have the Image Recognition option after upgrading, it can be added by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Rotor> Rotor Items and selecting Image Recognition. Since there are up to seven different options for Image Recognition, Apple has also given users the ability to add and remove what they wish to this rotor item. It can be configured by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Rotor> Image Recognition Rotor. Each of the available options will be discussed below. Image/Item Description will allow the user to get a description of the image or item that VoiceOver focus is set to. Based on my testing, it is generated in less than three seconds. It will be delivered in the form of a VoiceOver announcement. For those using braille, one can read the description at their own pace by pressing Space with N. When done, pressing space with n will return the user to where they were before. I find this particular function to be wonderful for generating descriptions of things in my Facebook feed, my growing photo library, album art in the Music app, and when reading photo-heavy articles on various news sources. Interestingly, this function is the only one that can be mapped to a Perkins-style keyboard. The other options discussed below are not available for users of Perkins-style keyboards. Using the Copied Speech Rotor option launched with iOS 26, users can copy the description to wherever they want on their iOS device. A simpler solution in some situations is available as discussed below. Ask About Image/Item is another option, which does exactly what the choice says. After selecting this, users are presented with a text field which allows them to type a question. Pressing return or enter will generate a response. The nice thing is that you do not need to generate a general description before asking a question. Placing VoiceOver focus on the image is all that is required. With many third-party applications, one must first wait through getting the general description before they can ask a question. I have solved simple CAPTCHAs by asking my iPhone to provide me with only the text in the image. I can then copy it and solve CAPTCHAs. I have not tried more complex puzzles. Explore Image/Item allows you to get the same description as you get when generating an Intelligent Description, but it is static text instead of a VoiceOver announcement. After the text description, there is an option to ask a question either by typing or voice. Also, when focus is on the description, one can flick up with one finger, or use whatever alternative method, to copy the description. Ask About Screen allows the user to get a description of the screen on their iOS device. It functions the same as the Ask About Image/Item choice, but covers the entire screen. I've found this feature handy for understanding what buttons without labels do. This is far more preferable to activating the button to see what happens. The other two options are Describe Screen and Explore Screen. These work the same as the others documented above, only this applies to your entire screen instead of one item. I mentioned browsing photos above, and when in the Photos app, there is yet another rotor option available called Save Intelligent Image Description. When selected, this will add the description generated to the photo itself which will then be available later. A final setting is the ability to show a list of the recognition options discussed above. It does not have a touch screen gesture assigned to it, but the user can create one. On a Bluetooth keyboard, pressing VoiceOver Modifier, Shift, and R will bring up this menu. Sorry, braille display users, there appears to be no Perkins-style keyboard option. Automatic Image Descriptions Users can head to Settings>Accessibility>VoiceOver>VoiceOver Recognition>Image Descriptions to configure whether image descriptions are provided automatically. One can configure whether they want automatic image descriptions or whether they are conveyed as a fall-back option to when images have alt text. Note that this setting applies to the classic image descriptions, but one will not recieve a etailed description such as the ones provided by Apple Inteligence. Braille There are some changes to braille outlined below. As a general usage note, writing longer passages of text seems to be a bit more reliable than it was in all of the iOS 26 releases. Further, there were some issues in iOS 26 with cursor routing buttons not routing correctly and focus jumping back to the top in longer blocks of text while the user was reading. Based on my use, all of these issues have been improved significantly. Predict More Predictably with Braille Screen Input Braille Screen Input now uses the same Predictive Text gestures as the default onscreen keyboard. When typing on the standard touchscreen keyboard, iOS uses Autocorrect and Predictive Text to identify the word you probably intended based on the letters entered, nearby keys, sentence context, and commonly-used language. Braille Screen Input now uses this same prediction system: after entering a word, users can swipe up or down with one finger to move through suggested words or corrections, then continue typing once the desired suggestion is selected. Further, it is now possible to type part of an emoji name and swipe up or down with one finger to find it. Functionality of the BSI Autocorrect requires the primary software keyboard Autocorrect setting to be enabled in Settings> General> Keyboards. Finally, iOS 27 adds the ability to more easily insert alternative characters. To activate alternative character selection, hold the dots of the character you wish to insert until you hear a sound, then release and swipe up or down with one finger to select the desired symbol. A More Flexible Cursor Shifting to braille display users, there is a new setting called 'Snap To Print Text Cursor', which can be found by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Braille> Cursor Routing. The options are the new Snap To Text Cursor or Any Braille Cell. By default, Snap To Print Text Cursor was selected when I upgraded. The 'Snap to Print Text' setting places the cursor on the closest print text equivalent even when contracted braille is enabled. This setting is particularly helpful for those braille display users using QWERTY keyboards to type while also using contracted braille for reading, as it removes some ambiguity from where the cursor is located. Text Field Labels That Stick Prior to iOS 27, when activating a text field, the text label would disappear entirely. In iOS 27, the label persists even when the text field is active. The label itself appears between two indicator symbols which clearly distinguish the label from the text entered. It can be configured by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Braille> Text Field Labels. The options are to show an abbreviated version of the label or the full thing. Selecting 'Collapse' will provide two indicators without the text label. Selecting 'Full' will display the entire text field label. You can collapse the label by pressing a cursor routing button. If you disable everything in this menu, the behavior will be as it always was in past versions of iOS. Braille Access Expands File Support Braille Access now supports plain text and PDF files. As such, the formerly named 'BRF Files' is now simply called 'Files'. To import these file types, users can follow the same procedures they already use to get BRF content imported. Files are still stored in the 'BRF files' folder on iCloud, so any method a user would utilize to copy text and PDF content is the same. I found that opening plain text files worked quickly, and it was nice to have them imported. Unlike many applications for braille readers, Braille Access tends to remember the place I was in a file when I open it again. PDF content will display, but seems to depend on how well the creator of the file treated accessibility. Formatting such as headings is not preserved. New Features Bring New Keyboard Shortcuts Apple has added a few new options for Perkins-style keyboard shortcuts that people may take advantage of. Under the VoiceOver category, one has been added for launching the Ask function found in VoiceOver Recognition, while another was added for generating an Intelligent Description with Image Recognition. There are no new commands for the other Image Recognition options discussed above. Another mapping option was made available for ignoring trackpads. Hearing ON-demand Sign Language Interpreters on FaceTime As part of Apple's Global Accessibility Awareness Day announcement in May, the company shared preliminary details of an API that providers of sign language interpretation apps could use to allow callers to add an interpreter to their FaceTime call. As of the time of writing, there do not appear to be any announcements concerning providers utilizing this API, but hopefully that will come soon. Auto-Caption This Video Captioning automatically produces synchronized subtitles from spoken audio when a video has no existing captions. Apple says it works with videos recorded on the iPhone, videos sent to the user, streamed videos, and other uncaptioned videos played through supported system playback interfaces. When I enabled captioning in the Photos app while playing a video, there were several visual options available for adjusting the output. However, I was not able to find the generated captions with braille. Thankfully, Live Captions under Braille Access works well. Conclusion iOS 27 may not bring as many accessibility changes as its predecessor, but several of its additions are substantial. The expanded image-recognition tools can give blind users faster and more independent access to photos, unfamiliar controls, and other visual information, while the new navigation and customization options allow VoiceOver users to better tailor the experience to their needs. Braille users also gain welcome improvements, including more reliable text editing, clearer text-field labels, and support for additional file formats in Braille Access. Some of the most significant new features require Apple Intelligence, leaving users of older compatible devices without access to everything discussed in this article. There are also a few places where braille keyboard support remains incomplete. Even with those limitations, iOS 27 offers a useful collection of accessibility improvements. As always, individual experiences will vary, and readers are encouraged to share their own observations and bugs in the comments. I also encourage users to check out the AppleVis list of bugs and fixes. If needed, more information on how to update the software on your device is available on this Apple Support page.

en.title: Final Fortress
en.summary: Final Fortress is a match-3 puzzle. The whole game is the screen of an old terminal: green text, one cursor, and you, the commandant of the last fortress. It is a quiet game. A working console in the dark, the hum of the systems, static like rain. A watch takes fifteen or twenty minutes: do the day's tasks, read what came in, hand over. Nothing hurries you, and nothing happens while you are away. Come back after a week and the fortress is exactly as you left it. Match tiles to finish the day's tasks. Each task brings supplies. Spend them to repair the fortress: reactor, hydroponics, antenna, armory, infirmary. Every repaired system opens new missions. Match 4 or more to charge special tiles. They clear a line, a block, or every tile of one kind. Swap two charged tiles together and they fire as one bigger shape, up to the whole board. The board gets busier as you go: convoy crates that pay out at the bottom, sealed containers with a special tile inside, interference to clear layer by layer, burned sectors the tiles fall past. Some tasks ask for a pattern: decode a sequence in order, or fill a gauge in every column. AI Madness is a mode of its own, outside the fortress. Each shift bends the rules: boards up to 10 by 13, sometimes only three kinds of tile, cascades that barely stop, tasks that may be impossible. On an iPhone with Apple Intelligence, Apple's on-device model (Foundation Models) picks the shift's character and writes its line in the log. Nothing leaves the phone. Otherwise the terminal does the same on its own. Nothing is at stake and nothing is banked. Every shift has a code. Send it to a friend and they get exactly the same board. There is a story in the log: three acts, four threads, and the notes of the commandants who held the fortress before you. It comes a few lines at a time. Read it or skip it. The game never nags about it. Repair the antenna and you will see a board with other players' stations. It is view-only, there is no chat, and it updates once a day. When the story is over, the log keeps going quietly on its own. The music belongs to your fortress alone. The sound is synthesized live and seeded from your fortress, so your station hums like no other and never loops. The hum changes with what is running, with the hour of the night and with the weather outside. Each kind of tile has its own note, and a cascade climbs the scale. One extra room, The Long Dark, carries a call of its own. Three more stations use the instruments in your phone: a weather post that reads the barometer, an acoustic modem and a direction finder. A home screen widget shows your fortress at a glance, in StandBy too. No ads. No lives, timers, energy or streaks. No pop-ups, no push notifications, no accounts, no daily rewards to come back for. Run out of moves and the terminal just says the packet was lost. Try again, nothing is taken away. You can drop a task at any time. Purchases are cosmetic only: screen colors, one extra soundtrack, custom names. Nothing you can buy helps you play, and no purchase moves you up the board. Works offline, on iPhone and iPad. Fully playable with VoiceOver, with a flicker-free stable phosphor mode and a calm mode that softens the board's flashes and haptics.

en.title: One Line Journal app
en.summary: One sentence a day. One book at the end of the year. Your life is happening — quietly, quickly, in small moments. One Line, One Year captures 2026 as it unfolds and turns it into a beautifully structured book that's entirely yours. HOW IT WORKS Daily — Write one sentence about your day. That's it. Weekly — Once a week, reflect in 3–5 sentences. Your daily entries appear above for context, so nothing gets lost. Monthly — Write a brief summary that becomes a full chapter in your book. Book View — Watch your year assemble itself in real time — months as chapters, weeks and days woven beneath them. Export — At year's end, export your complete book as Markdown, PDF, or DOCX. BUILT FOR PRIVACY Everything stays on your device. No accounts. No cloud sync. No analytics. Face ID and passcode lock keep your words yours — and auto-lock kicks in the moment you leave the app. THOUGHTFUL DETAILS Highlights to mark the moments worth remembering Tags to thread themes across your year Gentle reminders to keep the habit alive A clean, distraction-free writing interface Simple timeline navigation — no clutter, no feed NO SOCIAL. NO NOTIFICATIONS. NO NOISE. Just you and your words, building something you'll want to read. A year feels long while you're living it. It feels short when you look back. Capture it — one sentence at a time.

en.title: Surprise and Shine: Recapping Apple's September 9 Announcements
en.summary: Intro Apple has just wrapped up Surprise and Shine, the big fall announcement event. We got new iPhones, Apple Watches, and (non-pro) AirPods. And yes, the rumors were finally true: one of the new iPhones is a folding one. AirPods have some new tricks, the new Apple Watch has some very nice improvements, and even the normal iPhones are worth checking out. Let's get into it. iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo All of the iPhones announced today share a few features, so we'll start there. At the heart of each new iPhone is the A20 Pro, a system on a chip (SoC) that's better than anything Apple has ever made. So said the presenters, anyway. This is Apple's first 2NM chip, which basically means they shrank the parts so they can fit more into the same amount of space, all while using less power and producing less heat. The A20 Pro comes with four efficiency cores and two cores meant to do serious work, which is the same distribution as last year (six cores, with four efficiency and two powerful ones). The big change here is that the two workhorse cores, called super cores, are beefed up considerably. Apple claims they have desktop performance. The graphics chip has also been upgraded, with seven cores and faster access to the phone's RAM; Apple says graphics run up to 40% faster than the A19 Pro. It's 2026, so we can't not talk about AI, specifically large language models. The A20 Pro has neural accelerators to boost AI performance for the CPU and GPU cores, but the star of the show is the neural engine. Or rather, the engines, plural. Each A20 Pro has two of them, not just one, giving the chip 32 neural cores to work with. Combined with the A20's increased access to memory, Apple said that this is the best chip for mobile AI tasks. All of this performance is going to produce a lot of heat, so Apple took the vapor chamber from iPhone 17 Pro and made some improvements. The way the chip's components transfer heat to the chamber is more efficient now, the materials have been updated, and the design has been altered. The new design has three times the space and is made from a combination of titanium and a special copper alloy. It transfers 40% more heat than the system on iPhone 17 Pro, letting the phone do more work for longer before it has to slow itself down to keep from overheating. Remember Siri AI, a version of Siri that is aware of your locations, messages, and other details? It was announced back in June. If you don't follow Apple news as obsessively as I do, the short version is that Siri is far more aware and capable than before. You can ask for "that recipe Jake sent me a couple months ago", you can issue more natural commands, and you can get much more accurate results with dictation. All of this is kept in a new Siri app, so you can check on past conversations. Oh, and Siri's voice is better than ever. Anyway, Siri AI is fully supported by all the new phones, and Apple spent some time reminding us of what all is going to be possible. There are some extra goodies for Apple Watch Series 12 owners who have Siri AI devices, too, but we'll get to those later. iPhone 18 Pro As has become customary, Apple is offering this year's pro phones in standard and Max variants. The Max has the most battery life of any iPhone ever, while the smaller phone has battery life equivalent to what iPhone 17 Pro Max offers. This seems to be the main difference; both have the same chip, camera, design, and everything else, so I'll just talk about iPhone 18 Pro from here on out. Everything also applies to iPhone 18 Pro Max unless I say otherwise. The stand-out feature of the camera system this year is variable aperture. Specially-designed, tiny pieces in the camera can move to let in more or less light, which also changes the field depth. The aperture widens in low light, closes some in bright light, and can be manually adjusted to change the feel of a picture. I guess professional photographers will be jumping for joy. The A20 Pro's AI capabilities also allow Apple to add more camera enhancements, some of which we knew about already from the iOS 27 announcement at WWDC back in June. What is unique to iPhone 18 Pro, though, is a new set of manual camera controls, called pro controls. These let you change the aperture, white balance, and other settings whose purpose I can only guess at. You can even use AI to keep video locked on a subject. But you're not here for camera details, so let's get on with it. There are a few other, smaller changes compared to iPhone 17 Pro. The new phone can charge faster when plugged in (as opposed to using wireless charging). The Dynamic Island is also smaller and now supports up to three live activities at once. Surprisingly, that's about it. The battery life improvements are great, the A20 Pro sounds like an impressive chip, and the colors have changed (silver, black, glacier, and burgundy). Aside from that, faster wired charging, and the camera improvements, everything seems to be the same. Apple didn't mention the screen, body material, any new or changed buttons, speakers, wifi performance, or anything else. It seems iPhone 18 Pro is, physically, the same as iPhone 17 Pro, just with a new chip and camera. You can pre-order iPhone 18 Pro starting September 12, and it will start shipping on September 18. The Pro starts at $1,199, $1,299 for the Pro Max. This gives you 256GB of storage, just like last year. You can upgrade all the way up to 2TB of storage, the first time any iPhone has offered such a large internal drive. Just know that it won't be cheap. You can also check out the new array of colors for Apple's official cases, cross-body straps, and (new this year) wrist straps. iPhone Duo Apple's first entry into the world of foldable phones is called iPhone Duo . It has a 5.4-inch outer display and unfolds to show a 7.6-inch screen. Both screens have full Apple Pencil support, and the outer screen has Ceramic Shield 2. The frame is high-grade titanium, colored either white or night sky. The side button acts how you expect, but also sports a Touch ID sensor--the phone lacks Face ID. You can add multiple fingers, so that no matter how you happen to hold the phone, the finger resting on the button can unlock it. You can also unlock your phone with your watch. Also, despite being foldable, iPhone Duo has an IP68 rating. That means dust and water will have a hard time getting into it, but you shouldn't take it swimming. Each half of iPhone Duo is very, very thin--after all, the whole package has to be comfortably thin when folded. Apple says that each half is the thinnest iPhone ever produced, which suggests that the halves are thinner than an iPhone Air. Despite this, iPhone Duo has good battery life (30 hours of video playback on the internal screen, 44 when using the outer one) and supports fast wired charging. It also, as mentioned earlier, has the same A20 Pro chip and vapor chamber cooling as iPhone 18 Pro. It even has Apple's custom cellular modem, the C2, giving it millimeter wave 5G support (U.S. only for now) and faster and more efficient cellular communications overall. The camera situation is interesting. iPhone Duo sports the same camera system as iPhone 18 Pro, though without the variable aperture feature. When unfolded, an under-screen selfie camera is available, while a more capable camera lives just above the outer screen. This enables some neat options, such as letting both the photographer and the subject see the camera feed (one person on the inner screen, the other on the outer one) before a picture is taken. If you are taking pictures of children, iOS lets you enable animations designed to draw attention and get the kids' eyes looking toward the lens. When making FaceTime calls, someone can use the inner camera and screen, while someone else can use the outer set, letting two people use the same phone but with different camera feeds. Thanks to its design, you can fold iPhone Duo in such a way that the camera stays pointed where you want without being held. You can let iOS monitor the feed, and take the picture when it thinks you're ready. As to the screen, Apple spent a lot of time talking up the engineering that went into minimizing the crease, getting the under-finger feel right, and more. A special coating makes the screen feel closer to glass than the plasticky feel some folding phones have, while also cutting glare and reflections. Nano-scale layers of lenses help the screen stay bright and readable, while reducing the wear of all the folding and unfolding it will undergo during its life. That's not all the engineering that went into iPhone Duo, either. The frame is not only made of titanium, but reinforced at key points with custom materials for added strength. The hinge is weighted, balanced, and carefully structured to fully support the screen at every point of the folding process. You can set the two halves at any angle (up to 180 degrees) and they will stay there. Use it like a small iPad, set one screen at an angle like a laptop while you type on the other one, or make a tent shape, using the phone like a stand while you watch the outer display. The phone will react how you expect, even going so far as to constantly balance the audio coming from its dual speakers based on how the two halves are configured. iOS 27 has been designed to take full advantage of this phone's unique abilities. You can do a lot of the multi-tasking tricks that you can on iPad, such as opening two apps side by side, quickly moving between on-screen apps, showing a list of emails and an open message at once, and more. You can see two home screen pages at once, and your dock is now vertical. Video controls now appear on the side of the screen, rather than the bottom, so videos have more space and so your thumb can reach the controls. The status bar is smaller and now stays in a corner, again, to give apps more room. Apps have new APIs available, letting them, for example, show a list of options on one half of the screen and a preview of the selected option on the other half. iOS will even detect how the phone is being used and move content toward the edge, so it is easier to tap or see. I realize that much of this section has been about cameras, on-screen layouts, and other things that a lot of you reading this won't care about. That's because that was the focus of the presentation. For now, iPhone Duo feels like a device that will be amazing for plenty of sighted users, but will have less appeal to those of us who use VoiceOver. Low vision folks may love the larger screen, but not being such a person myself, I can't really comment on that. Personally, I'm going to see how things go with this phone, play with one in person once my local stores have some, and not worry about getting my own just yet. I don't know if there will be enough advantage for VoiceOver to justify the cost. Of course, it would be nice to have Touch ID again. iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model. As with iPhone 18 Pro, you can increase this all the way to 2TB. Preorders open on October 16, with deliveries and in-store availability starting on October 23. AirPods 5 Today brought us a new AirPods model: AirPods 5 . Like the previous generation, they come in two variants, one more expensive than the other. With AirPods 4, the cheaper model lacked active noise cancelation and wireless charging. That's not the case anymore With this new generation, both variants have ANC. The more expensive AirPods add volume adjustment on the stem, just like AirPods Pro, and a case that supports wireless charging. As we've come to expect, the case can handle MagSafe, Qi, and Apple Watch chargers. The premium version also have a five-hour battery life, which is an hour more than what the less expensive ones offer. This is measured with ANC enabled. Both versions of AirPods 5 are, Apple claims, designed to feel and sound better while lasting longer. ANC is 50% more effective than AirPods 4, while transparency sounds more natural. Audio sounds more detailed and rich, and the earbuds can shrug off more sweat and rain than before. They will also work better in even more ear shapes--so Apple says, anyway. No, they are still not available in any color other than white. The less expensive AirPods cost $129, which is what the non-noise-canceling AirPods 4 cost, and this generation includes ANC. That's a good deal, but for just $20 more, you can get on-stem volume controls and a case that can charge wirelessly. That's $149, which is $30 less expensive than the high-end AirPods 4. Apple isn't known for lowering prices, so this is a very pleasant surprise. You can pre-order starting today (September 9). Deliveries will begin arriving September 18, which is also when stores will start offering the new AirPods. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 The Apple Watch got some nice enhancements this time around. They all apply equally to the Series 12 and Ultra 4, so I will just talk about the new features here. Everything is true of both models, neither of which seems to have changed, physically, from its predecessor. The first improvement is to the heart sensors. Apple Watch has always used lights to measure your pulse, and that hasn't changed. The LEDs in these new models are different, though. Skin contact is better, the LEDs have been arranged in a ring pattern, and the color of the light has gone from red to green. Add in the new electrical sensors for ECG readings, and Apple Watch has never had a more accurate measure of your heart rate. Almost more exciting is how often Apple Watch now takes heart measurements: every five seconds. This is up to sixty times more often than previous Apple Watches did. Heart rate variability (HRV) is now measured every five minutes, which is a 24 times increase. HRV is an indicator of stress and cardiovascular health, so the more (and more accurate) the readings, the better. This generation of watch has better step length tracking as well, meaning that indoor walks and runs will be measured more accurately than before. Apple also claims that this makes Apple Watch the most accurate step tracker of all the modern wearables. They are therefore adding a step count complication, at long last. What will watchOS do with all this data? Apart from your heart rate complication actually showing your current pulse, Apple has made a series of health data improvements. A readiness score suggests whether you should make today a recovery-focused day or a day during which you can push more. On iPhone, your heart and activity data feed a new Longevity feature. You can see how you are doing over time, how your metrics compare to the average person at your age, and what you could do to improve things. To make this feature more accurate, you can take VO2 max, flexibility, movement, and other tests, all done using your iPhone's cameras and live coaching from the app. You can also purchase bloodwork from Quest for $119, directly through the Health app (U.S. only, for now). The results will inform your health insights and recommendations. You can also connect your existing health records, as has been possible for some time. It's not all about health, though. Audio Intelligence is a set of features centered around the microphones in the watch and Siri AI's increased abilities. All of these features are opt-in, meaning they are not enabled by default. Sound Recognition has been on iPhones for years, but now comes to Apple Watch. People who are deaf or hard of hearing can be alerted to sirens, alarms, doorbells, and other sounds. This works even without iPhone nearby. Live Rewind: double press the digital crown and you get a transcript of the last fifteen seconds of conversation. You can read it, or choose to send it to Siri for further use. During the presentation, they showed a server listing food options, then an Apple Watch user bringing up the list as a transcript. It's not clear if you have to activate this feature each time you want the watch to start paying attention, or if it is always available. Siri Recap is a feature you turn on when you want it, such as during a business meeting or an important conversation. Once the event is over, you turn Recap off again. Siri will generate a title and key points from what it heard, letting you review what was said and jog your memory. I assume this also adds to Siri AI's context, letting you ask questions about what was said in the meeting last week, for instance. Shazam for song detection is nothing new, but it is now automatic (once you turn the feature on). You can always know what song is playing near you, without having to ask Siri to do anything. Apple promised that all of these features run locally or, when they don't, are end-to-end encrypted and have extra security built in. No speakers are ever identified or tagged, no audio is saved, nothing is used for training AI. In fact, audio processed by Apple Watch can't leave the system because of how the S11 SoC is designed. Apple has a whole privacy paper about Audio Intelligence if you want to read more. Speaking of the S11 system, let's go over what we know, which isn't much. We know it has something called an Audio Exclave, which is where audio from the watch's microphones is saved and processed. Audio can't leave this isolated part of the system, which is part of how Apple guarantees that Audio Intelligence puts privacy first. The S11 also supports the greatly increased health sensor readings without impacting battery life. Beyond that, Apple made no claims about speed increases, wireless changes or anything else. In a bit of a surprise move, Apple has kept prices the same. The Series 12 starts as $399 for the aluminum casing, while the Ultra starts at $799. Preorders are open today (September 9) and, as with most of what we've talked about here, deliveries and in-store availability start on September 18. The new colors and materials are: aluminum, now with Ceramic Shield 2 glass: black, space gray, light gold, and dark bronze ceramic: pearl white and night blue titanium (Series 12): radiant gold and natural titanium (Apple Watch Ultra 4): black and natural That's All For Now Rumors continue to swirl that Apple has more to show us, so there might be press releases or another event later this year. For now, though, we've covered all the new shinies--iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Plus, version 27 of all of Apple's operating systems comes out on September 14, at which time we will finally get a look at this much-improved Siri that all these new devices were built to support. What caught your metaphorical eye, if anything? Personally, I pre-ordered a Series 12 before I was halfway done writing this article. It'll be a big upgrade over my SE 3, and since most of what I use my Apple Watch for is health-related, I want all the data I can get. I might see about AirPods 5 if a good sale comes along, but I'll wait for the reviews. I like the idea of a folding phone, and I definitely want to play with one in person, but I have no desire to own one. I'm also not planning to get an iPhone 18 Pro, though if Siri AI and upcoming Apple Intelligence features turn out to be as amazing as Apple insists they are, well, we'll see. What do you think? Discuss your excitement, bitter disappointment, or indifference in the comments!

en.title: Apple Introduces Updated Mac Mini and Mac Studio with Upgraded Chips and Improved Connectivity
en.summary: Apple today updated the Mac mini and Mac Studio, introducing the M6 Chip for the Mac mini, as well as the M5 Ultra Chip for the Mac Studio, which Apple describes as its "most powerful silicon ever." Mac mini The new Mac mini with M6 delivers up to 4x faster AI performance, up to 2x faster graphics and storage, and Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and 2.5 gigabit Ethernet connectivity, according to Apple's press release for the Mac Mini . Apple lists the following additional claims related to the Mac Mini with M6: Up to 13.5x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac mini with M1, and up to 4.8x faster than M4. Up to 2.3x faster spreadsheet calculations in Microsoft Excel when compared to Mac mini with M1, and up to 1.5x faster than M4. Up to 2x faster gaming performance with ray tracing in Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition when compared to Mac mini with M4. In addition to the M6, the Mac mini is also available with M5 Pro, which Apple claims delivers: Up to 8.5x faster LLM prompt processing performance in LM Studio when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 4x faster than M4 Pro. Up to 4.5x faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 1.4x faster than M4 Pro. Up to 2.1x faster image processing in Affinity when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 1.5x faster than M4 Pro. Besides the upgraded chips, the new Mac mini features Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and 2.5GB Ethernet by default (up from the prior generation's default 1GB Ethernet port), with a 10GB option available. The new Mac mini can be preordered from Apple today for a starting price of US $899, and will begin shipping on Tuesday, September 22. Mac Studio Apple has also updated the Mac Studio, bringing the M5 Max and new M5 Ultra chip to Apple's most high-end Mac, as well as Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6 connectivity, and a "next-generation SSD architecture that is up to twice as fast as before," according to Apple's press release for the Mac Studio The new Mac Studio with M5 Max delivers up to 3.9x faster AI performance than the prior generation, with the M5 Ultra delivering up to 4.3x the peak AI performance of the M3 Ultra, and up to 9.8x the peak AI performance of the M1 Ultra. Apple additionally lists the following claims related to Mac Studio with M5 Max: Up to 10.7x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and 3.9x faster than M4 Max. Up to 7.4x faster text-to-image performance when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 3.5x faster than M4 Max. Up to 5.3x faster Magic Mask performance in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 3x faster than M4 Max. Up to 3.5x faster basecalling for DNA sequencing in Oxford Nanopore MinKNOW when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 1.9x faster than M4 Max. In addition to the M5 Max, the new Mac Studio is available with the new M5 Ultra, which Apple claims delivers: Up to 15.4x faster CopyCat ML training performance in Foundry Nuke when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 3.3x faster than M3 Ultra. Up to 9.8x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 4x faster than M3 Ultra. Up to 8.2x faster text-to-image performance when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 4.3x faster than M3 Ultra. Up to 4.7x faster scene rendering performance in Maxon Redshift when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 1.7x faster than M3 Ultra. In addition, the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra is available with up to 512 GB of unified memory with 1.2TB/S of memory bandwidth, 50% higher memory bandwidth than M3 Ultra. The new Mac Studio can be preordered from Apple today for a starting price of US $2,499, and most models will begin shipping on Tuesday, September 22, with the model with 512GB of memory shipping in late October.

Muy atentos. Hoy les traigo la actualización de TCA-TTS-TIMMER, nuestro querido reloj parlante para Windows, que llega a la versión 1.2 cargada de novedades muy importantes y funcionalidades útiles! Antes, para quienes no lo conozcan: ¿Qué es TCA-TTS-TIMMER? Es una pequeña utilidad desarrollada en Python que nos permite escuchar la hora cada 15 minutos, 30 minutos o cada hora, mediante un sonido y una voz TTS. Además, puede darnos la hora de muchos países de Latinoamérica y Europa, todo desde una interfaz sencilla, totalmente accesible y con atajos de teclado. Novedades en TCA-TTS-TIMMER 1.2 El reloj llega a la versión 1.2 con los siguientes cambios: • Hora Universal UTC Ahora el reloj incorpora un botón en la interfaz principal que te permite saber la Hora Universal UTC al instante. Disponible también mediante el atajo de teclado Alt+U. Muy útil para quienes trabajan con sistemas, servidores o simplemente necesitan la referencia horaria internacional. • Nueva voz: Español México (mx) Además de la voz español España, ahora incorporamos la voz español México (mx). Podrás elegir entre ambas desde el cuadro combinando "Lenguaje de la voz" en las opciones. Descargador de Música Accesible 1.4.2 : Otra gran alternativa inclusiva para YouTube Introducción En el mundo actual, el contenido multimedia es parte fundamental de nuestro día a día. Para la comunidad de personas con discapacidad visual, contar con herramientas que permitan descargar y gestionar este contenido de forma autónoma es vital. Si bien ya existen en el ecosistema opciones consolidadas y muy queridas como TCA MediaDownloader, siempre es una excelente noticia recibir nuevas propuestas que enriquezcan nuestras opciones. Hoy queremos hablar de Descargador de Música Accesible, otra fantástica alternativa que se suma a la lista de herramientas diseñadas desde cero para garantizar una experiencia fluida, cómoda y sin barreras. Esta aplicación ha sido desarrollada por Nicolás Alfaro, programador y miembro del colectivo de personas con discapacidad visual, quien ha puesto su conocimiento al servicio de la comunidad. ¿Qué es Descargador de Música Accesible? Es una aplicación gratuita para Windows que permite bajar audio y video desde YouTube de manera sencilla y con total compatibilidad con lectores de pantalla. Actualmente en su versión 1.4.2, el programa destaca por su ligereza y por integrar soluciones prácticas —como un reproductor interno portable— que facilitan la navegación previa a la descarga. Al ser un proyecto creado por y para usuarios con discapacidad visual, cada ventana y comando está optimizado para responder exactamente a lo que la comunidad necesita, convirtiéndose en un complemento ideal para tu día a día digital. Características principales • Interfaz 100% accesible: Diseñada minuciosamente para funcionar a la perfección con NVDA y JAWS. Cada elemento, botón y cuadro de diálogo está correctamente etiquetado para una navegación fluida mediante el tabulador y atajos de teclado. • Buscador integrado de YouTube: No necesitas abrir el navegador. El programa incluye una pestaña de búsqueda directa que ofrece hasta 50 resultados, permitiéndote elegir el contenido exacto desde una lista cómoda y accesible. • Reproductor interno MPV: Una de las novedades más potentes de la versión 1.4.2. Incorpora un reproductor basado en MPV portable para escuchar el audio o ver el video antes de descargarlo, con controles adaptados y accesibles. • Variedad de formatos y calidades: Audio (MP3): Permite elegir entre calidades de 128, 256 y 320 kbps. Video (MP4). • Información detallada antes de descargar: Puedes verificar el título, duración, fecha de publicación y número de visualizaciones para asegurarte de que es el archivo correcto. • Historial de descargas: Un registro organizado y accesible desde el menú superior para revisar tus archivos obtenidos recientemente. Mantenimiento y actualización integrada: Como YouTube actualiza su plataforma constantemente, el programa incluye una opción en el menú de herramientas para actualizar las librerías de yt-dlp de forma automática, garantizando que el software nunca quede obsoleto. • Sistema de diagnóstico: Si experimentas fallos con el lector de pantalla o el reproductor, la app cuenta con una herramienta de diagnóstico que verifica el estado de NVDA y los módulos de Python. Puedes exportar este reporte para recibir soporte técnico de forma eficiente. Contacto y soporte El desarrollo de software accesible crece gracias a la retroalimentación de la comunidad. Si tienes sugerencias, comentarios o deseas reportar algún fallo, puedes ponerte en contacto directo con el desarrollador: Correo electrónico: alfaronico8@gmail.com Nota para el soporte: Se recomienda ser lo más detallado posible al describir cualquier incidencia o sugerencia para facilitar las futuras actualizaciones del programa.
